attackPath.dataflow: stored owner data -> ProgressRecord -> CSV cell -> spreadsheet
attackPath.impact: Operator spreadsheet execution or deceptive links.
attackPath.reachability: A user can supply stored owner text before an operator opens the report.

codeEvidence.code: row := []string{fmt.Sprintf("%d", r.OwnerID), r.OwnerName, r.Status, fmt.Sprintf("%d", r.TagsAdded), fmt.Sprintf("%d", r.TagsFailed), r.ErrorMessage}; cw.Write(row)
codeEvidence.explanation: OwnerName and ErrorMessage reach CSV cells without formula neutralization.
codeEvidence.label: Unsanitized report cells

confidence.rationale: Source-to-sink trace is direct and a neighboring CSV exporter implements the missing control.

findings.remediation: Apply a shared CSV-cell sanitizer to every untrusted textual report field before calling csv.Writer.
remediationTests: Add a table-driven reporter test for values beginning =, +, -, and @ in both owner and error fields.

rootCause.summary: The report writer relies on CSV quoting but does not apply the leading-character neutralization required for spreadsheet consumers.

severity.changeConditions: Severity rises if the report is automatically distributed to broader recipients.
severity.rationale: Stored data can trigger spreadsheet execution only when an operator runs the migration and opens its report.

findings.summary: The operator CSV report writes stored owner names and error messages directly, allowing leading spreadsheet formula markers to be interpreted when the report is opened.
findings.title: LSTEP migration report permits spreadsheet-formula injection

validation.counterevidence: The report is an operator-run artifact.
validation.evidence: Owner.Name is copied into ProgressRecord and a neighboring exporter has sanitizeCSVCell for this precise control.

attackPath.dataflow: authorized fractional treatment request -> DecreaseStock -> int conversion -> zero/truncated decrement
attackPath.impact: Stock availability, clinical supply, and financial records diverge.
attackPath.reachability: Any treatment creator can select an inventory ID and submit a fractional quantity.

codeEvidence.code: func (r *repository) DecreaseStock(ctx context.Context, clinicID, id uint64, quantity float64) error { qty := int(quantity); ... UpdateColumn("quantity", gorm.Expr("quantity - ?", qty)) }
codeEvidence.explanation: Converting a positive fractional quantity to int yields zero before both the stock guard and decrement.
codeEvidence.label: Truncating stock decrement

confidence.rationale: The exact float-to-int conversion is visible on the path from HTTP request to atomic update.

preventiveControls: Use one domain quantity type for treatments and inventory.
findings.remediation: Either reject non-integral quantities for integer-stock items before creating the treatment, or store and atomically decrement inventory using a precise decimal representation.
remediationTests: Assert that quantity 0.5 is rejected or decrements precisely and that 1.5 cannot under-decrement stock.

rootCause.summary: The treatment quantity type and inventory quantity semantics are inconsistent, with loss of precision at the enforcement point.

severity.changeConditions: Severity rises if fractional quantities are valid for regulated or high-value supplies.
severity.rationale: A clinic staff member authorized to create treatments can defeat stock accounting and availability checks for inventory-backed medical items.

findings.summary: Inventory-backed treatments accept fractional quantities, but stock decrement truncates the value to an integer before enforcing availability and updating stock.
findings.title: Fractional treatment quantities bypass inventory decrement

validation.counterevidence: The action is clinic-scoped and permission-protected, but those controls do not preserve stock integrity.
validation.evidence: float64 input is forwarded unchanged into int(quantity); Go conversion is deterministic.

attackPath.dataflow: repository read access -> account identities and bcrypt verifiers -> offline credential attack or local/test deployment access
attackPath.impact: Staff privacy and privileged local/test account security are weakened.
attackPath.reachability: All repository readers can obtain the tracked seed material.

codeEvidence.code: 実スタッフの氏名・email・password hashなどのPII/credential verifierをseedやGit履歴へ追加しない。
codeEvidence.explanation: The repository explicitly defines the tracked data as prohibited.
codeEvidence.label: Seed-data policy

confidence.rationale: The tracked CSV, migration plan, and policy are explicit; no credential value was exposed in this report.

preventiveControls: Run secret and PII scanning on seed exports before commit.
findings.remediation: Replace tracked identities and verifiers with synthetic disabled fixtures, and provision any necessary local accounts through a secret-managed one-time path.
remediationTests: Add a seed-content test that rejects active privileged accounts, email addresses, and password-hash columns or values in tracked demo bundles.

rootCause.summary: Privileged local/test identities and password verifiers are committed rather than provisioned through a non-versioned local or secret-managed path.

severity.changeConditions: Severity rises if any demo credential, identity, or seed bundle is reused in a release environment.
severity.rationale: Repository readers receive data usable for offline password attacks or test-environment access; production and staging have a seed-selection mitigation.

findings.summary: The local/test demo seed stores active system-admin account rows, staff email identities, and bcrypt password verifiers in the repository despite the repository policy prohibiting that material in seeds or Git history.
findings.title: Tracked demo seed exposes privileged-account verifiers and staff identity data

validation.counterevidence: Production and staging migration plans exclude the bundle.
validation.evidence: The CSV contains active admin metadata and verifiers, and the development/test migration plan loads 003_demo.

attackPath.dataflow: compromised registry artifact -> npx execution -> runner secrets -> exfiltration or Worker modification
attackPath.impact: Cloudflare and staging database credential compromise.
attackPath.reachability: The manually dispatched workflow runs with staging secrets.

codeEvidence.code: CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and staging DB secrets are exported before npx -y wrangler@4.107.0 secret put commands.
codeEvidence.explanation: Registry-fetched code executes with the deployment token and database credentials available.
codeEvidence.label: Credentialed npx execution

confidence.rationale: The secret environment and npx execution are adjacent in the workflow.

findings.remediation: Install Wrangler through a frozen lockfile and invoke the resolved local binary, or verify a downloaded artifact against a maintained digest before exposing secrets.
remediationTests: Add a workflow policy check rejecting npx or npm remote execution in secret-bearing steps.

rootCause.summary: A secret-bearing workflow resolves executable package code outside the repository's lockfile and without artifact verification.

severity.changeConditions: Severity rises if the token is production-wide or the workflow becomes reachable by untrusted code.
severity.rationale: A substituted package can exfiltrate a Cloudflare deployment token and staging database credentials, though exploitation requires compromise of the external package-distribution path.

findings.summary: The staging Worker secret-sync job downloads and executes Wrangler through npx in the same step that exposes Cloudflare and database secrets, without a lockfile or artifact-digest integrity binding.
findings.title: Secret-sync workflow executes an unverified npm artifact

validation.counterevidence: The named package version and normal npm transport reduce but do not remove artifact-substitution risk.
validation.evidence: The workflow exports secrets and calls npx twice in the same step.

attackPath.dataflow: compromised package trust path -> runner code execution -> later credentialed k6 process
attackPath.reachability: The performance workflow installs and later invokes k6 with staging credentials.

codeEvidence.code: curl https://dl.k6.io/key.gpg | sudo apt-key add - && sudo add-apt-repository ... && sudo apt-get install k6
codeEvidence.explanation: Neither an expected signing-key fingerprint nor a package version/digest is enforced.
codeEvidence.label: Unpinned k6 installation

confidence.rationale: The package installation and later credentialed commands are explicit in one workflow.

preventiveControls: Keep secrets unavailable until after verified tool setup where possible.
findings.remediation: Use a version-and-digest-pinned k6 artifact or image, or verify a known signing-key fingerprint and exact package version before installation.
remediationTests: Add a CI policy test rejecting apt-key, unversioned privileged package installs, and unverified remote keys.

rootCause.summary: The workflow extends its package trust root dynamically without binding it to an expected key or artifact.

severity.changeConditions: Severity rises if the workflow handles production secrets.
severity.rationale: A compromised external key, repository, or package can run code on the hosted runner before credentialed k6 commands, but requires upstream distribution compromise.

findings.summary: The performance workflow imports a remote APT key through apt-key, installs an unversioned k6 package, and later runs it with staging demo credentials.
findings.title: Performance workflow trusts an unpinned k6 installation path before credentialed execution

validation.counterevidence: The runner is ephemeral and HTTPS/signing are present, but expected provenance is not pinned.
validation.evidence: The subsequent k6 commands receive staging demo credentials.

attackPath.dataflow: compromised action tag -> runner action code -> deployment credentials -> release or credential compromise
attackPath.impact: Deployment credential or release integrity compromise.
attackPath.reachability: Both deployment workflows execute the tags before credentialed commands.

codeEvidence.explanation: These semantic version tags are not immutable commit references.
codeEvidence.label: Backend action tags

confidence.rationale: The action tags and later credentialed commands are directly visible in both workflows.

preventiveControls: Scope tokens minimally and protect deployment environments.
findings.remediation: Pin every third-party Action in privileged workflows to a full commit SHA and use an automated reviewed updater for SHA changes.
remediationTests: Add a workflow lint rule requiring full SHA pins for third-party actions in secret-bearing jobs.

rootCause.summary: Privileged workflows trust mutable external action labels rather than reviewed, immutable action revisions.

severity.changeConditions: Severity rises if the workflows become reachable from untrusted pull requests.
severity.rationale: A compromised or retargeted upstream Action tag can execute on a runner before Cloudflare or Vercel credentials are used; this requires a third-party publisher compromise.

findings.summary: Backend and frontend deployment jobs execute checkout, pnpm setup, and Node setup through version tags rather than immutable commit SHAs before credentialed deployment commands.
findings.title: Deployment workflows use mutable third-party Action references

validation.counterevidence: The actions are reputable and versioned, but their tags remain retargetable.
validation.evidence: Deployment actions run before Cloudflare or Vercel token use.
